title: Top 5 Weirdest Ways Animals Sleep 😴
hook: You think you sleep badly? Wait until you see how these 5 animals do it.
script:
You think you sleep badly? Wait until you see how these five animals do it.
We're counting down to the strangest sleeper on the planet.
Number five: sea otters.
They float on their backs and often hold paws, so they don't drift apart.
Number four: sperm whales.
They nap upright, like giant floating pillars, for just ten to fifteen minutes.
Number three: the common swift.
This bird can stay airborne for about ten months straight, and scientists think it naps up there.
Number two: frigatebirds.
Researchers caught them sleeping mid-flight, in bursts of about twelve seconds.
That adds up to less than an hour a day.
Number one: wild African elephants.
A study found they sleep only about two hours a day, mostly standing up.
So the strangest sleeper of all? The giant that barely sleeps.
Which one sleeps most like you? Comment below.
And next time you think you sleep badly, wait until you see how these five animals do it.

title: 5 Funny Town Names With Wild Backstories

script:
These five real town names sound made up, but you could drive to every single one of them.
Every name has a true story.
Number five: Accident, Maryland.
Two survey teams in the seventeen-fifties measured the same land by mistake. Hence, Accident.
Number four: Hot Coffee, Mississippi.
A shop owner sold hot coffee to travelers, and the town took the name.
Number three: Why, Arizona.
It sits where two highways form a Y. But names needed at least three letters, so Y became W-H-Y.
Number two: Truth or Consequences, New Mexico.
In nineteen-fifty, a radio show offered to broadcast from any town that took its name. Hot Springs said yes.
Number one: Boring, Oregon.
It's officially partnered with Dull, Scotland, and Bland, Australia. Yes, really.
So the funniest name? Boring. Which is anything but.

title: The Great Rubber Duck Escape of 1992 🦆
hook: A storm knocked 28,800 bath toys off a ship, and they ended up teaching you how the ocean moves.
script:
A storm knocked twenty-eight thousand eight hundred bath toys off a ship, and they ended up teaching you how the ocean moves.
Here's how they became a science experiment.
It's January, nineteen ninety-two.
A cargo ship from Hong Kong hits a storm in the North Pacific.
Containers tumble into the sea, and one is full of plastic toys.
Yellow ducks, blue turtles, red beavers and green frogs.
The box breaks, and they float away.
Ten months later, the first ones wash up in Alaska.
Ocean scientist Curtis Ebbesmeyer gets curious.
He asks beachcombers to report every toy.
Each sighting shows where the currents carried them.
Some circled the North Pacific in a giant loop of current, and some may have drifted into the Arctic ice.
So a lost box of bath toys helped map how the ocean moves.
Found one on the beach? What would you name it? Tell me below.
Because a storm knocked twenty-eight thousand eight hundred bath toys off a ship…

title: 3 School Facts That Are Actually False
hook: 3 facts you probably still believe, and you have 3 seconds to guess which are false.
script:
Three facts you probably still believe, and you have three seconds to guess which are false.
Say true or false out loud before the timer runs out.
Fact one: goldfish only remember things for three seconds.
Three, two, one.
False! Scientists have trained goldfish to respond to sounds and remember them for months.
Fact two: you can see the Great Wall of China from space with your bare eyes.
Three, two, one.
False again! From orbit it's very hard to spot, because it's narrow and the same color as the land around it.
Fact three: bulls get angry when they see the color red.
Three, two, one.
Also false! Bulls can't see red the way you do. It's the cape's movement that gets their attention.
So the answer: all three are false.

title: 3 Memory Tricks to Remember Anything
hook: If you've ever forgotten someone's name 5 seconds after hearing it, you need these 3 tricks.
script:
If you've ever forgotten someone's name five seconds after hearing it, you need these three tricks.
They come from real memory research.
Trick one: test yourself instead of rereading.
In one famous study, students who quizzed themselves remembered more a week later than students who just reread.
Meet someone? Say their name back, then recall it a minute later.
Trick two: chunk it.
Your brain juggles only a handful of things at once, so phone numbers come in little groups.
Long code? Shopping list? Break it into chunks of three or four.
Trick three: build a memory palace.
Picture your home, and put each thing you want to remember in a different room.
Memory champions use it, and in one study, regular people who practiced got way better at lists.
That's the set: test yourself, chunk it, and build a memory palace.
Which trick are you trying first? Tell me in the comments.
Because if you've ever forgotten someone's name five seconds after hearing it…

title: Is That Really What I Sound Like?
hook: You've never actually heard your own voice. Not once. Here's why.
script:
You've never actually heard your own voice. Not once. Here's why.
Not the way everyone else hears it, and it's down to your skull.
When you talk, your voice reaches your ears in two ways.
First, through the air, just like any other sound.
Second, through your own head. The vibrations travel through the bones of your skull, straight to your inner ear.
And bone is great at carrying the low, deep parts of your voice.
So to you, your voice sounds richer and a bit deeper.
A recording only catches the air part. No skull, no extra bass.
That's why it sounds higher and thinner, and kind of not like you.
So, is that really what you sound like? Yes. The recording is much closer to what your friends hear every day.
And that voice you cringe at? They already love it.
Be honest, do you skip your own voice messages? Tell me in the comments.
Because you've never actually heard your own voice…

title: 5 Peppers That Make Jalapeños Look Mild
hook: You think jalapeños are hot? The pepper at number one is hundreds of times hotter.
script:
You think jalapeños are hot? The pepper at number one is hundreds of times hotter.
Let's count down five peppers that make a jalapeño look mild.
Pepper heat is measured in Scoville units, and a jalapeño is only a few thousand.
Number five: the habanero. Up to around three hundred fifty thousand.
Already way too much for most people.
Number four: the ghost pepper. Around one million.
It was the first pepper ever measured over a million.
Number three: the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion. Around one point two million, with a little stinger-like tail.
Number two: the Carolina Reaper. About one point six million.
It held the world record for about ten years.
Number one: Pepper X. About two point seven million.
That's the hottest pepper in the world, according to Guinness.
Please, admire these with your eyes, not your mouth.
What's the hottest thing you've ever eaten? Tell me below.
And if you think jalapeños are hot…

title: The Cave Found by 4 Teenagers in 1940
hook: What would you do if you found a hole in the ground with 17,000-year-old paintings inside?
script:
What would you do if you found a hole in the ground with seventeen-thousand-year-old paintings inside?
In nineteen-forty, four teenagers in France actually did. Here's what happened.
It's September, near the village of Montignac.
Teenager Marcel finds a hole. The story goes, his dog Robot led him there.
Days later, he returns with three friends and a lamp.
They squeeze down into the dark.
The walls are covered in hundreds of painted animals. Horses, bulls, deer, in red, yellow and black.
They'd found Lascaux, with paintings around seventeen thousand years old.
Soon, crowds of visitors came.
But all that breath and body heat started damaging the paintings.
So in nineteen sixty-three, the cave was closed to the public.
Today, visitors see exact replicas instead.
Four teens, one lamp, and one of the greatest art discoveries ever.
What would you paint for people seventeen thousand years from now? Tell me below.
And what would you do if you found a hole in the ground…

title: 3 Tricks to Cut Onions Without Crying
hook: You're probably making the onion tears worse, and here's how to fix it with 3 tricks.
script:
You're probably making the onion tears worse, and here's how to fix it with three tricks.
First, the reason it happens.
When you cut an onion, you break open its cells.
That sets off a reaction that makes a stingy gas.
It floats up, hits your eyes, and your eyes make tears to wash it out.
Trick one: chill it first.
Pop it in the fridge before cutting. Cold slows the reaction, so less gas reaches your eyes.
Trick two: use a really sharp knife.
A dull knife crushes the onion, and crushed cells release more of the stuff. A sharp blade slices clean.
Trick three: leave the root end for last.
That part is packed with more of the tear-making compounds, so cut around it.
That's it: chill it, sharpen it, and save the root for last.
Bonus: swimming goggles. They work, and look hilarious.
Which trick are you trying next time? Tell me below.

title: Wrinkly Fingers Explained in 60 Seconds
hook: You've had pruney fingers 100s of times, but the reason is actually your nervous system.
script:
You've had pruney fingers hundreds of times, but the reason is actually your nervous system.
Most people blame water soaking in. Here's the clue that says otherwise.
Doctors noticed that if the nerves in a finger are badly damaged, that finger doesn't wrinkle at all.
So it's not just soaking. Your nervous system is doing it.
After a few minutes in water, it tells the tiny blood vessels under your fingertips to tighten.
Your fingertips shrink a little underneath.
And the skin on top folds into those wrinkles.
But why would your body do that?
One idea is grip.
In one experiment, wrinkly fingers moved wet marbles between boxes faster.
Kind of like tire treads on a rainy road.
Scientists are still testing that idea, but it's a pretty cool one.
So next bath, you're not getting pruney, you're getting grippy.
What did you think caused it? Tell me in the comments.
